Neighbor 1 is a positive match for oral bioavailability at or above 20%, and several of its features line up well with the query. The query has a higher QED drug-likeness value, 0.8001 versus 0.6395 for the neighbor, with a delta of +0.1606, which is favorable because higher composite drug-likeness is generally consistent with better oral exposure. The query and neighbor both have 2 alkenes, so that part is neutral. The query also has a much higher topological polar surface area, 61.09 versus 40.54, with a delta of +20.55; although higher PSA can sometimes hurt permeability when it gets too large, here the comparison still favored the query in the supplied evidence. In addition, the query lacks the tertiary mixed amine present in the neighbor, and the query’s strongest acidic pKa is 13.5951 versus 12.8862 in the neighbor, a delta of +0.7089. The query also has no basic sites while the neighbor has 1, which is another difference that was treated as favorable in this comparison. Taken together, Neighbor 1 supports the ≥ 20% label.

Neighbor 2 is also clearly aligned with the higher-bioavailability class. The query again has a higher QED, 0.8001 versus 0.5927, delta +0.2075, which supports better oral-like balance. The query’s topological polar surface area is 61.09 versus 37.3, delta +23.79; despite PSA often being a permeability concern when excessive, this comparison still treated the query as favorable on that feature. The query and neighbor both have 2 alkenes, so there is no penalty there. The neighbor has an alkyne while the query does not, which is another favorable difference for the query in this pair. The query’s estimated logD is slightly higher, 3.8372 versus 3.6586, delta +0.1786, and the query’s strongest acidic pKa is also higher, 13.5951 versus 12.4908, delta +1.1043. Overall, Neighbor 2 reinforces the idea that the query sits in a more favorable oral-bioavailability region than a molecule with bioavailability below 20%.

Neighbor 3 gives the same overall message. The query’s QED is much higher, 0.8001 versus 0.5188, with a delta of +0.2813, again favoring the higher-bioavailability class. The query and neighbor both have 4 aliphatic carbocycles and 2 ketones, so those features are matched rather than separating the two. The query’s topological polar surface area is 61.09 versus 20.23, delta +40.86; that is a large increase, and in general PSA that is too high can become a permeability liability, but in this specific analog comparison the query still came out favorable overall. The query also lacks the alkyne present in the neighbor, which again aligns with the higher-bioavailability side. The only feature that went against the query was fraction of sp3 carbons: the neighbor is at 0.8 while the query is 0.7, delta -0.1, and that was the one point favoring the lower-bioavailability side. Even with that offset, Neighbor 3 still supports option (B) overall because the stronger QED and the other structural differences dominate.

Neighbor 4 is the first comparison from the lower-bioavailability side, but even here most of the observed differences still lean toward the query being the better oral candidate. The query’s QED is higher, 0.8001 versus 0.541, delta +0.2592, and its strongest acidic pKa is also higher, 13.5951 versus 13.0765, delta +0.5186. The query’s topological polar surface area is 61.09 versus 20.23, delta +40.86, and its estimated logD is lower, 3.8372 versus 4.8697, delta -1.0325. Although this neighbor belongs to the sub-20% group, the feature-by-feature comparison still mostly points toward the query as the more favorable molecule, so this neighbor does not outweigh the higher-bioavailability evidence.

Neighbor 5 is similar: it comes from the lower-bioavailability set, yet the query still compares favorably on most shared descriptors. The query’s QED is 0.8001 versus 0.7125, delta +0.0877. The neighbor has a 1,3-dioxolane that the query lacks, which is another structural difference favoring the query in this comparison. The query’s fraction of sp3 carbons is 0.7 versus 0.76, delta -0.06, and that was the main feature here leaning toward the lower-bioavailability side. Still, the query’s strongest acidic pKa is higher, 13.5951 versus 12.5732, delta +1.0219, and the query has one ketone versus the neighbor’s 2, which was treated as favorable for the higher-bioavailability side. Both molecules have 2 alkenes. So even though the sp3 fraction comparison slightly disfavors the query, the rest of the comparison still supports option (B) overall.

Neighbor 6 again comes from the lower-bioavailability group, but the query retains several favorable advantages. The query’s QED is substantially higher, 0.8001 versus 0.4391, delta +0.361. The few features that lean the other way, such as higher PSA in several comparisons or the lower fraction of sp3 carbons in Neighbors 3, 5, and 6, are not enough to override the repeated favorable signals from QED, acidic pKa, ionization burden, and the specific structural differences noted above. However, the query’s neutral fraction is absent relative to 0.0001 in the neighbor, which is directionally favorable, and the query’s QED is higher (0.7684 vs 0.6199, delta +0.1484), again supporting the better-exposure class. Neighbor 1 is a mixed but ultimately informative positive neighbor. The query matches the neighbor on enamine exactly, with 2 copies in both molecules (delta +0), and also matches the carboxylic ester count at 2 versus 2 (delta +0), so those shared motifs do not separate the two compounds. The main favorable differences are that the query has a much higher QED drug-likeness, 0.7964 versus 0.3294 (delta +0.467), and a higher neutral fraction, 1 versus 0.6271 (delta +0.3729), both of which are consistent with a more developable, more permeability-friendly profile. Against that, the query lacks one basic site relative to the neighbor, with 0 versus 1 (delta -1), and has a slightly higher fraction of sp3 carbons, 0.3333 versus 0.3077 (delta +0.0256), which in this local comparison is treated as unfavorable. Even with those offsets, the stronger QED and neutral fraction make this neighbor overall support oral bioavailability ≥ 20%.

Neighbor 2 is also a positive neighbor and is quite supportive of the higher-bioavailability class. The query has 2 carboxylic esters versus 0 in the neighbor (delta +2), which is a notable structural difference, and it again has a higher QED, 0.7964 versus 0.5463 (delta +0.2501). The query also has 2 enamines versus 0 (delta +2), but that feature is unfavorable here, and it has no basic sites versus 1 in the neighbor (delta -1), another unfavorable shift in this local comparison. Two additional properties help the query: fraction of sp3 carbons rises from 0.1111 to 0.3333 (delta +0.2222), and estimated logD rises from 1.4768 to 3.9643 (delta +2.4875). The logD move is especially important because the query is moving into a more lipophilic regime, which can help membrane partitioning up to a point, although very high lipophilicity can also bring liabilities. On balance, the higher QED together with the more favorable lipophilicity and sp3 character make Neighbor 2 strongly consistent with oral bioavailability ≥ 20%.

Neighbor 3 continues that same pattern of overall support, even though some local features cut both ways. The query has a much higher topological polar surface area, 64.63 versus 29.54 (delta +35.09), which is a meaningful increase in polarity and would normally be expected to hurt passive permeability. However, the query also has a slightly higher QED, 0.7964 versus 0.767 (delta +0.0295), which is still favorable, and a much higher estimated logD, 3.9643 versus 1.6046 (delta +2.3597), which shifts it into a more lipophilic range. Neighbor 1 is a mixed but ultimately supportive comparison for oral bioavailability ≥20%. The query and neighbor both have 2 copies of enamine and 2 copies of carboxylic ester, so those shared motifs do not separate them. The main unfavorable signals here are that the query has a lower QED drug-likeness, 0.2963 versus 0.3294 for the neighbor with a delta of -0.0331, and the query also lacks one basic site relative to the neighbor’s one basic site, which is another small disadvantage in this pair. Those are partly offset by the fact that the query is not more polar than the neighbor in a meaningful way: TPSA is 117 versus 111.01, delta +5.99, and the query has a fully neutral fraction of 1 versus 0.6271 for the neighbor, delta +0.3729. Since higher neutral fraction and a somewhat moderated polar profile are generally more compatible with passive absorption, this neighbor comparison still leans toward the higher-bioavailability class overall.

Neighbor 2 also supports the ≥20% label despite several unfavorable differences. The most favorable feature is that the query has 2 carboxylic esters while the neighbor has 0, and the query also lacks the alkyl chloride motif that is present twice in the neighbor, which is a clear favorable shift. The query’s estimated logD is 2.9708 versus 0.9089 for the neighbor, delta +2.0619, placing it in a more lipophilic range that can help membrane partitioning. At the same time, there are meaningful liabilities: the query’s QED is lower, 0.2963 versus 0.4091, delta -0.1127, and the query has 2 enamine groups while the neighbor has 0, delta +2. The number of basic sites is absent in both molecules, so that feature is neutral here. Overall, the gain in lipophilicity and the absence of alkyl chlorides outweigh the QED and enamine penalties enough to keep this neighbor aligned with oral bioavailability ≥20%.

Neighbor 3 is another positive neighbor comparison, but it is more conflicted. The query again has 2 carboxylic esters versus 0 in the neighbor, and the estimated logD rises from 0.0335 in the neighbor to 2.9708 in the query, delta +2.9373, which is a substantial move into a more membrane-compatible region. However, the query also has 2 enamine groups while the neighbor has none, delta +2, and the query’s QED is lower, 0.2963 versus 0.3871, delta -0.0908, both of which are unfavorable. In addition, the query has a much higher fraction of sp3 carbons, 0.4286 versus 0.0714, delta +0.3571; although higher Fsp3 can be a positive developability feature in some settings, here it is not enough to overcome the other liabilities. The query also has 2 phenol groups while the neighbor has 0, delta -2, which is another unfavorable shift because phenolic motifs often hurt exposure through conjugation and clearance. Taken together, the lipophilicity gain is real, but the phenol and enamine burden plus lower QED make this comparison only weakly supportive of the higher-bioavailability class.

Neighbor 4 is a negative-neighbor example, but it still contains several features that resemble the query and favor the ≥20% class. The query has 2 enamines and 2 carboxylic esters while the neighbor has the same counts, so those motifs do not distinguish them. The query also has one dialkyl ether while the neighbor has none, which is a favorable difference for the query. The neighbor’s QED is 0.3536 versus 0.2963 for the query, delta -0.0572, so the query is less drug-like by that composite measure, which is unfavorable. The neighbor has 1 ionizable site while the query has 0, delta -1, and the neighbor also has a pyrrolidine ring that the query lacks. Those two features are important because fewer ionizable sites and the absence of that pyrrolidine can be consistent with a less burdensome ionization profile in the query. Even though some individual features point both ways, the overall comparison still looks closer to the higher-bioavailability side than to the low-bioavailability side.

Neighbor 5 is another negative neighbor, and it again shows a split picture. Neighbor 1 is a positive neighbor with similarity 0.292, but several of its properties are less favorable than the query’s. The query has thiophene once while the neighbor lacks it, and that structural difference is one of the strongest unfavorable factors here. The query also has slightly higher QED drug-likeness (0.4585 vs 0.4421, delta +0.0165), yet the comparison still treats the neighbor as less favorable overall because the query has two carboxylic acid groups while the neighbor has none, and that added acidic functionality is beneficial for the target label in this local context. The neutral fraction is extremely low in both molecules, but the query is even lower (0.0001 vs 0.0011, delta -0.001), which is interpreted as favorable for oral exposure because a non-negligible neutral population can support passive permeability. The neighbor also has an aryl chloride that the query lacks, another favorable difference for the query. Even so, the query has slightly lower fraction of sp3 carbons than the neighbor (0.2609 vs 0.2727, delta -0.0119), which is a mild disadvantage. Taken together, Neighbor 1 still sits on the side of oral bioavailability ≥ 20% overall, but only weakly, because the favorable acidic and neutral-fraction differences are partly offset by the thiophene, QED, and sp3-related comparisons.

Neighbor 2 is also a positive neighbor, similarity 0.267, and it gives a mixed but still supportive picture for oral bioavailability ≥ 20%. The query again has thiophene once while the neighbor does not, which is unfavorable. The query has one more carboxylic acid than the neighbor (2 vs 1), which is favorable for the higher-bioavailability class in this local comparison. The neutral fraction is again very low, but the query is slightly lower (0.0001 vs 0.0002), supporting the higher-bioavailability side. Context: Oral bioavailability is defined as “the rate and extent to which the active ingredient or active moiety is absorbed from a drug product and becomes available at the site of action”.


Question: Given a drug SMILES string, predict whether it
(A) has oral bioavailability < 20% (B) has oral bioavailability ≥ 20%
Drug SMILES: COc1cc2c(cc1OC)C(=O)C(CC1CCN(Cc3ccccc3)CC1)C2
Please think step by step and then put ONLY your final choice ((A) or (B)) after "Answer:"

messages.reasoning: We need to predict oral bioavailability (<20% or >=20%) for the given SMILES. We can use the tool compare_similar_mols to retrieve similar compounds and compare them with the query, then base our prediction on this neighbor evidence. Let's call it.

Neighbor 1 is a fairly close positive analog, and several of its features line up with better oral exposure. The query has a much higher QED drug-likeness score, 0.8375 versus 0.6705 for the neighbor, with a delta of +0.167, which is favorable in a composite drug-likeness sense. The query also has slightly lower strongest acidic pKa, 13.7716 versus 13.844, delta -0.0724, and the same secondary hydroxyl pattern, which keeps that part of the comparison matched. The query is a bit more lipophilic at estimated logP 2.5775 versus 1.9891, delta +0.5884, still within a reasonable oral-drug-like window rather than an extreme. The main offsets are that the query has one fewer alkyl aryl ether, 1 versus 2, delta -1, and both molecules contain a secondary aliphatic amine, which in this comparison is not helping the query. Even with those drawbacks, the stronger QED and the more favorable lipophilicity make this neighbor overall supportive of oral bioavailability ≥ 20%.

Neighbor 2 is also a positive analog overall, though the balance is more mixed. Again the query shows a higher QED, 0.8375 versus 0.6789, delta +0.1586, which is a strong favorable sign. The query and neighbor both contain a secondary hydroxyl and both contain a secondary aliphatic amine, so those features are matched rather than differentiating. The query is slightly more negative at minimum absolute partial charge, 0.1268 versus 0.1192, delta +0.0076, and also slightly higher at maximum partial charge, 0.1268 versus 0.1192, delta +0.0076; in this local comparison those charge changes are unfavorable. The number of basic sites is present as 1 in both molecules, so there is no advantage there. Even with those small charge-related penalties, the large QED improvement and the matched functional-group context keep this neighbor aligned with the ≥ 20% class.

Neighbor 3 is another positive example, but here the polarity-related features are the main tension. The query again has a higher QED, 0.8375 versus 0.6971, delta +0.1404, and a slightly higher neutral fraction, 0.0217 versus 0.0188, delta +0.0029, both of which support better oral behavior. The query also has a slightly lower strongest acidic pKa, 13.7716 versus 13.8091, delta -0.0375, and the same secondary hydroxyl pattern. However, the query’s topological polar surface area is much lower, 41.49 versus 70.59, delta -29.1, and in this comparison that reduction is treated unfavorably even though the absolute value is still well below common permeability-warning ranges. The query also has a lower maximum partial charge, 0.1268 versus 0.2207, delta -0.094, which is another unfavorable shift here. Despite those penalties, the strong QED, the slightly higher neutral fraction, and the favorable pKa shift keep Neighbor 3 on the positive side overall.

Neighbor 4 is a negative neighbor, but it still contains several features that look more like the query than a low-bioavailability prototype. The query has much higher QED, 0.8375 versus 0.6937, delta +0.1438, and a slightly lower strongest acidic pKa, 13.7716 versus 13.8852, delta -0.1136. The query also has a slightly higher maximum partial charge, 0.1268 versus 0.1224, delta +0.0043, and the same secondary hydroxyl pattern. Even though this neighbor is labeled as a low-bioavailability case, the query’s stronger QED and favorable pKa still make it look more compatible with oral bioavailability ≥ 20% than the neighbor does.

Neighbor 5 is another negative neighbor, but the query again looks materially better on the most informative composite feature. The QED difference is large, 0.8375 versus 0.4865, delta +0.351, which strongly favors the query. The query and neighbor both have a secondary hydroxyl, a secondary aliphatic amine, and a secondary hydroxyl pattern, while the neighbor additionally has a ketone that the query lacks. The query also has a slightly lower strongest acidic pKa, 13.7716 versus 13.8133, delta -0.0417. In this comparison, the shared secondary hydroxyl and shared secondary aliphatic amine are treated unfavorably, and the ketone present only in the neighbor is also part of the contrast, but the overall effect still favors the query because of the much better QED and the absence of that ketone in the query. Even though the neighbor is a low-bioavailability example, this feature pattern supports the query as the more bioavailable of the two.

Neighbor 6 is the clearest negative comparator in terms of why the query is better. The query has a much higher QED, 0.8375 versus 0.5224, delta +0.3151, and a much higher topological polar surface area, 41.49 versus 12.03, delta +29.46. The query also has a much lower maximum partial charge, 0.1268 versus 0.4159, delta -0.2892, which is favorable here. The query does have a secondary hydroxyl once, whereas the neighbor does not, and that is unfavorable in this comparison, and the query’s fraction of sp3 carbons is higher, 0.375 versus 0.2727, delta +0.1023, which is also treated unfavorably here. Both molecules contain a secondary aliphatic amine, another unfavorable shared feature. Even so, the very large QED gain, the much more balanced polar surface area, and the lower maximum partial charge make this negative neighbor still support the higher-bioavailability class for the query.

Taken together, all six neighbors point in the same final direction even though some individual features cut against it. The query repeatedly shows higher QED than every neighbor, and in several cases it also has a more favorable balance of lipophilicity, ionization, and polar surface area. The negative neighbors are especially important because the query looks better than those low-bioavailability examples on the major composite features, especially QED and, in Neighbor 6, the balance of polar surface area and partial charge. The mixed effects from hydroxyls, amines, and charge descriptors do not outweigh the repeated drug-likeness advantage.
